newsitem.title: INDIA: India looks down foggy road to freeing oil sector.
newsitem.headline: India looks down foggy road to freeing oil sector.

text.p: India Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's vow to erase a multi-billion dollar debt to oil companies and slash petroleum subsidies will open the way for the sector's deregulation, analysts said on Friday.
But they were unsure how he would do it.

There were too many unanswered questions to Gujral's grand plan for the oil sector, but the end goal would be to free the companies from an administered pricing mechanism and throw the sector open to competition, they said.
Until the ruling United Front's policy-setting steering committee finally decides what to do about oil prices and a $5.3 billion debt to companies, analysts could only speculate.
"Everything is up in the air until the next steering committee meeting," P. Dhileepan, oil analyst at NatWest Markets in Bombay, told Reuters.
That meeting has been deferred three times so far, after two inconclusive earlier meetings. There is no confirmation of a new date, and official sources said July 17 is being talked about.
Urgent action is needed. Oil refiners are facing a credit crunch, and have told the government that unless it stumps up money soon there will be no cash in their kitty to buy crude.

New Petroleum Minister Janeshwar Mishra drove the point home on Thursday. "Under the present circumstances, imports may dry up," he said. Indian Oil Corp, the country's sole importing agency, has already borrowed 140 billion rupees ($3.9 billion) and is owed 90 billion from the oil pool.
Gujral, in an interview with state-run Doordarshan television later on Thursday, said subsidies on liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and diesel would be slashed.

He also said the government was willing to transfer the outstanding bill to oil companies --which was put at 190 billion rupees ($5.3 billion) in the interview-- for sales of petroleum products onto its own account.
"If they are able to all this, one of the biggest impediments to de-control will be removed," another oil sector analyst, who requested anonymity, said.
But Gujral gave few hints how he would do the job.
"We will find a way out. And this is what we are trying to build a concensus on. Let me hope I will succeed," he said.
Subsidy cuts on diesel and LPG are considered fairly simple.

NatWest's Dhileepan said a 15 percent hike in diesel prices would bring India virtually in line with international prices, and LPG prices, currently 40-50 percent below international levels, could be hiked 20-25 percent without too much pain.
But adding billions of dollars to the government's fiscal deficit to take the oustanding burden off companies for selling oil products below market prices was a tall order, they said.
The oil pool deficit ballooned after a surge in world prices last year, as home prices were left unchanged. At the end of 1996/97 (April-March), the deficit stood at 155 billion rupees.

Finance Minister P.Chidamabaram has so far fought off "tremendous pressure" to get him to take the oil deficit onto the government's books, officials said. Currently, the deficit is hived off and administered by an Oil Coordination Committee.
Chidamabaram's target of cutting the fiscal deficit to 4.5 percent of gross domestic product in 1997/98 from 5.0 percent in 1996/97 would be jeopardised if he takes on the oil burden.

Advocates of the government taking on the deficit have proposed that bonds should be given to oil companies to cover the debt -- which the companies could sell either to the central bank or on the secondary market.
Gujral said there would be no increase in kerosene prices, which are most heavily subsidised, as this was the main cooking and lighting fuel for the masses of Indians living in poverty.
And it looks likely petrol will escape a price hike, also, as its prices are already pitched above international levels to help support India's complex cross-subsidy scheme. ($1=35.7 rupees)
